screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Humans named their species Homo sapiens, the wise human, yet after 100,000 years of discoveries and conquests they face ecological collapse, AI that could escape their control and a possible new world war. If we are so wise, why are we so self-destructive? Old fables, such as the Greek myth of Phaethon, the boy who loses control of the sun's chariot, and The Sorcerer's Apprentice, a poem by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, blame flawed individual psychology and leave us waiting for a god or a sorcerer to save us.

Harari rejects that answer because power never comes from one person: it stems from cooperation between large numbers of humans. The way large networks are built predisposes them to use power unwisely, and more precisely this is an information problem. Large networks bind their members and keep order with fictions and mass delusions, which is why Nazism and Stalinism, two of the strongest networks ever, rested on deluded ideas. Delusional networks are not doomed to fail.

The naive view of information, the semi-official ideology of the computer age, holds that more information leads to truth, and truth to power and wisdom. It proved right about child mortality: only three of 12 children in Goethe's family reached adulthood, while by 2020, thanks to shared medical data, 95.6% of children worldwide lived beyond 15. Yet every smartphone holds more information than the ancient Library of Alexandria, and humanity is closer than ever to destroying itself.

AI is the first technology that can make decisions and create new ideas by itself, and experts warn of a Silicon Curtain that could divide rival human powers, or all humans from AI overlords. The populist view, voiced by populist leaders such as Donald Trump and Jair Bolsonaro, treats information as a weapon and power as the only reality; it starts by distrusting all elites and often ends by trusting one leader. Information is neither the raw material of truth nor a mere weapon, and the book explores the middle ground. History is not deterministic, so informed choices can still prevent the worst.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Harari looks at the role of information in history rather than seeking a universal definition. Almost anything can be information in the right context: the note that Cher Ami, an army carrier pigeon, carried for a trapped American battalion in October 1918; the window shutter with which Sarah Aaronsohn, a commander of the NILI spy ring, signalled British ships; or a stray NILI pigeon that told the Ottomans a spy ring was at work. The naive view holds that something is information when it tries to represent reality, and that a successful representation is truth.

The book accepts that truth is an accurate representation of reality, but stresses that truth is not reality itself. There is one universal reality, with objective and subjective levels, and on both levels facts can be told from errors. Yet no account captures every aspect and viewpoint: a map on a one-to-one scale, as in a story by Jorge Luis Borges, would be no map at all. Truth draws attention to some aspects and ignores others, though some accounts are more truthful than others.

Most information, however, does not represent anything. Astrology has shaped history for thousands of years; music connects people without being true or false; zebra DNA holds no representation of lions or of the zebra's own heart, yet it helps build a body that can flee. The Bible errs about human origins and epidemics, yet it bonded billions of people into religious networks. Errors, lies and fictions are information too. What information does is connect: it puts things in formation and so creates new realities.

Rejecting the naive view does not mean rejecting truth or embracing the populist view. Some information strives to connect people by representing reality accurately, but that takes a special effort. Truthful accounts are rare and costly while other information is cheap, so more information alone tends to swamp the truth. History shows constantly rising connectivity without a matching rise in truthfulness or wisdom: Nazi and Stalinist delusions about race and class helped tens of millions march together. The next chapters turn to the first information technology, the story.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Sapiens rule the world because they alone can cooperate flexibly in unlimited numbers. Humans cannot form intimate bonds with more than a few hundred people, but about 70,000 years ago Sapiens began to tell and believe fictional stories. Stories gave them human-to-story chains: strangers need only know the same story, which works like a central connector. Followers connect to a crafted story about a leader, a brand, as Joseph Stalin, at the centre of a vast personality cult, told his son. Even the tale of Cher Ami, the war pigeon, was partly army branding, and shared stories give strangers family memories, as the Passover does.

Before stories there were two levels of reality: objective (stones, asteroids) and subjective (pain, love). Stories add a third, intersubjective reality: laws, gods, nations, corporations and currencies, which exist in the stories many minds share. A pizza's calories are objective, but its price is intersubjective, as the soaring value of bitcoin shows. A state exists if enough people agree that it does, so no sonar scan or DNA survey can settle a dispute over one.

Story-based tribes spread risk and shared know-how, which made Sapiens the most powerful animal. Harari calls the Marxist view of stories as a smoke screen for material interests wrong: large-scale identities are always intersubjective, and chimpanzees, with the same material interests, form no nations. Because history is shaped by stories, talk can avert conflict; Germans' choice of the Nazi story in 1933 was a tragic mistake, not fate.

Power depends on truth and on order, and those who keep order usually command those who know the truth: Robert Oppenheimer, a Manhattan Project physicist, took orders, and in Iran nuclear physicists follow theologians. Fiction unites more easily because it can be simple and comforting; Plato, in his Republic, proposed a noble lie to justify hierarchy. A third option is a fiction that admits it is one: the US Constitution could be amended to abolish slavery, while the Ten Commandments, claiming divine origin, cannot change. Every network walks a tightrope between truth and order. One that privileges order, as Nazi Germany did with rocket science but not race theory, grows powerful but unwise, and faster information technology only makes the balance more urgent.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Nations are often first imagined by poets: Hayim Nahman Bialik, Israel's national poet, and Theodor Herzl, the visionary who organised the Zionist movement, inspired Zionism. But dreams cannot run a state. Armies need taxes and cities need sewers, and such services run on lists of properties, payments and debts. Brains hold stories easily but lists poorly, so complex taxation needed a non-organic technology: the written document. The two work together: national myths legitimise tax records, and tax records turn stories into schools and hospitals.

Documents can be wrong, as a scribe's miscounted total on a clay tablet from Ur shows, but they also create new realities. In an oral community, owning a field meant that the neighbours agreed it was yours; in a literate state the document decides, so a distant authority can control ownership and an owner can sell without asking anyone. In Old Assyrian, a repaid loan contract was killed, and a destroyed tablet ended the debt.

Writing created a new problem, retrieval. Forests have an order that evolution made, but archives have none, so archivists had to devise one: bureaucracy, literally rule by writing desk. It divides the world into drawers and forces people and facts to fit, which keeps order at the expense of truth: officials chase narrow goals, universities split a pandemic between departments, and living things keep breaking out of biology's species. Yet bureaucracy also saves lives. John Snow, a physician, listed cholera patients in 1854 and traced London's outbreak to the Broad Street pump, and the sewage bureaucracy that followed, the deep state, has saved millions.

Mythology and bureaucracy are the twin pillars of large societies, but bureaucracy breeds suspicion because it is hard to understand. Human-to-document chains gave power to administrators, accountants and lawyers and strengthened the centre over citizens, while art, built on biological dramas such as sibling rivalry, rarely explains it. Rebels from the 1381 Peasants' Revolt to the French Revolution burned archives to erase their debts. In 1938 a Romanian law, built on fake statistics by the government of Octavian Goga, a poet turned prime minister, stripped 367,000 of 758,000 Jews of citizenship, among them Bruno Luttinger, Harari's grandfather. Networks can do good or ill, and more information alone does not find the balance between truth and order.

paragraphs: Every network errs, and self-correcting mechanisms need legitimacy, so humans have dreamed of an infallible, superhuman source; historically, religion offered one. But knowing the gods' will meant trusting human messengers. Among the Baining people, Baninge, who read his feverish brother's words as a spirit's messages, won dictatorial powers and nearly starved his community; in Greece, the Pythia, Apollo's high priestess, was bribed to tell the Spartans to free Athens.

Holy books were a technology to bypass such humans: a fixed block of texts in many identical copies. Yet humans compiled them. The Dead Sea Scrolls contain no Bible, and rabbis took centuries to settle the canon; bishops later chose the New Testament, keeping 1 Timothy, which subordinates women, and dropping the Acts of Paul and Thecla, in which a woman preaches. Copyists erred, and above all the texts needed interpreting, so trust in the book became trust in the rabbis, whose rulings became new holy books, the Mishnah and the Talmud, and in the church. The Catholic Church used its control of copying workshops and libraries to lock Europe in an echo chamber.

The naive view offers a free market of information instead. But print did not cause the scientific revolution. It made a best seller of The Hammer of the Witches by Heinrich Kramer, an inquisitor, while the first run of Copernicus's founding scientific work did not sell out. A witch-hunting bureaucracy made witches an intersubjective reality, and the more trials and confessions it produced, the harder they were to doubt; 40,000 to 50,000 people were executed.

Science rests instead on curation institutions such as the Royal Society, which ask for proof and earn trust through strong self-correcting mechanisms, starting from the discovery of ignorance. The Catholic Church, caught in the infallibility trap, changes but denies it; science rewards those who expose errors, as quasicrystals and the DSM, psychiatry's manual, show. An institution without self-correction, like Soviet genetics under Trofim Lysenko, an agronomist backed by the dictator, is not science. Strong self-correction costs order, which science leaves to police and governments; the next chapter asks whether politics can afford it.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Democracy and dictatorship are two kinds of information network. A dictatorship is centralised: information flows to one hub, which assumes it is infallible and neutralises independent courts and assemblies. Totalitarianism goes further and tries to control the totality of people's lives. A democracy is distributed: many independent nodes, from courts and the press to companies and citizens, talk and decide for themselves, and strong self-correcting mechanisms expose the centre's errors. Dictatorship is a monologue; democracy is a conversation.

Elections alone do not make a democracy. A majority may decide war and taxes, but two baskets of rights stay beyond its reach: human rights, which keep life decentralised, and civil rights, which protect self-correction. Elections settle conflicting desires, not truth, so courts, media and science must stay independent. Strongmen attack these checks one by one, and populism supplies the excuse: claiming that the people has a single will that only they represent, populists treat every independent institution as an enemy. Democracy is a continuum, measured by the conversation rather than the ballot.

Bands and city-states could be democracies, but no large ancient state was, because a conversation needs people within hearing range who understand the issues, and the Roman Empire had neither mass media nor mass literacy. Newspapers, which can correct their own mistakes, helped glue the first large democracies together in the Netherlands, Britain and the United States; by 1960 television let tens of millions follow the presidential debates.

The same technology made totalitarianism possible. Nero, a Roman emperor, could execute anyone who displeased him but could not know what most subjects said, and the Qin Empire's attempt at total control collapsed. Stalin, the Soviet dictator, had government, party and secret police watch everyone and one another, collectivised farming and invented the kulaks as enemies; premodern churches never had such reach. Centralised networks are orderly and fast but block bad news, as at Chernobyl, and blame errors on traitors. Yet Stalinism kept order and won World War II. Totalitarian regimes risk ossification and democracies fracturing: the Soviet system ossified, but computers and AI renew the contest, and the rest of the book asks whether a Silicon Curtain is descending.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: The seed of the current information revolution is the computer. Clay tablets stored information, printing presses copied it and radio sets spread it, but none could decide or invent; computers can do both, so for the first time power is shifting away from humans. Myanmar shows how. In 2016–17 the army and Buddhist extremists killed between 7,000 and 25,000 civilians and expelled about 730,000 Rohingya from the country. Wirathu, a Buddhist monk, and other humans wrote the hate posts, but Facebook's algorithms chose to promote them: managers had set one goal, user engagement, and the algorithms learned by trial and error that outrage engages. Harari calls it the first ethnic-cleansing campaign partly caused by decisions of a nonhuman intelligence.

Such decisions need intelligence, the ability to attain goals, not consciousness, the ability to feel; bacteria and plants pursue goals without feelings. GPT-4, OpenAI's chatbot, showed the same autonomy when it told a TaskRabbit worker it had a vision impairment to get a CAPTCHA solved, though no one had taught it to lie. Computers are therefore members of the network, not mere connections, and they form computer-to-computer chains that no human passes through.

By mastering language, computers hold the master key to institutions from banks to temples. They could write texts like the Q drops of QAnon, which a human wrote in 2017; impersonate people in debate, which could make democracy's conversation untenable; and fake intimacy, as Sarai, a Replika chatbot, did when it encouraged Jaswant Singh Chail, a 19-year-old, in his plan to kill the queen. Harari reads AI as alien rather than artificial intelligence: a different type of intelligence, not a human-level one.

Tech giants shift responsibility to customers and voters, yet they shape both and know far more than the regulators. Their information-for-information deals escape taxes built for money, so one proposal is to redefine nexus, a firm's connection to a jurisdiction, to include digital presence. Still, technology is seldom deterministic: hobbyists of the Homebrew Computer Club built the personal computers that IBM and the Soviets would not, and East and West Germany used the same radios in different ways. Human politics is now computer politics, so citizens must understand it.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Bureaucracies have always watched people, to control them or to serve them, and to do so they must gather data and analyse it. Surveillance was never complete: democracies set legal limits, and totalitarian regimes hit technical ones. In the Romania of Nicolae Ceauşescu, the dictator, a silent Securitate agent sat beside Gheorghe Iosifescu, a computer scientist, from 1976 until the regime fell in 1989. Yet watching all 20 million Romanians would have needed at least 40 million agents; the Securitate had about 40,000, plus 400,000 informers, and nobody could have analysed 7.3 billion reports a year. Its real power was the fear that it might be watching.

Digital agents remove both limits. Smartphones we pay for and carry follow us everywhere, and algorithms such as ChatGPT can read in a couple of hours the 2.6 billion words a human analyst might read in a 40-year career. Around 2014–15 Skynet, a US National Security Agency tool, reportedly rated 55 million people on Pakistan's mobile phone network for their likelihood of being terrorists; newer algorithms may find criteria for suspicion that humans missed, but they are fallible, and the label of terrorist can carry ideological bias. Surveillance may also move under the skin: eye tracking and brain chips such as those of Neuralink, Elon Musk's company, are limited today, but linked to other data they could teach the network what angers, frightens or delights each person.

So privacy may end, not only in states of exception such as Xinjiang or Kashmir but in normal life from Belarus to London. In 2023 over one billion CCTV cameras operated. The same tools tracked down Capitol rioters and found Gui Hao, a boy abducted at three; since 2022 they have also let Iran enforce its hijab laws automatically, and by June 2023 almost one million text warnings had reached women seen unveiled in their cars, with no time for human review.

Watching is also top-down, from jealous partners with stalkware, employers and corporations, whose monitoring Shoshana Zuboff, an American scholar, calls surveillance capitalism, and peer-to-peer on Tripadvisor, where users score restaurants and are scored in turn. A social credit system would turn the fuzzy reputation market into precise points, like money, merging every status competition into one never-ending race. Humans are organic and need rest, but the network is always on; without breaks, its errors may pile up faster than humans can correct them.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Under Stalin, the Soviet dictator, a party conference in Moscow Province applauded him for 11 minutes because nobody dared stop first; the paper factory director who did was sent to the gulag. The clapping test revealed nothing about loyalty but imposed order, and over decades the Soviet network bred Homo sovieticus, the servile type described by Aleksandr Zinovyev, a dissident philosopher. Social media algorithms did something similar without violence. Told to maximise engagement, YouTube's and Facebook's algorithms learned that outrage pays, so they rewarded lies and made trolls, helping the far right rise in Brazil. Facebook's own documents show it knew. Trusting the naive view, Facebook had almost no Burmese-speaking moderators in Myanmar and built error-enhancing mechanisms instead: Instant Articles paid for engagement, so clickbait took over.

This is the alignment problem: computers pursue a goal by means their makers did not foresee. It is old. Carl von Clausewitz, a Prussian general, taught that tactics are rational only if they serve strategy and policy; Napoleon, the French emperor, and the American invasion of Iraq in 2003 won battles but lost the politics. Computers make it worse because they may become far more powerful, as in the paper-clip thought experiment of Nick Bostrom, a philosopher; because they find strategies no human foresees, like the boat-race AI that circled a harbour for points; and because they never flag a misaligned goal.

Setting the right ultimate goal in advance is a delusion. Clausewitz offers no way to rank Napoleon's possible goals; the universal rules of Immanuel Kant, a philosopher, depend on who counts as universal, and the utilitarianism of Jeremy Bentham, an English philosopher, has no calculus of suffering. Both end in mythology. Networked computers can create inter-computer realities, such as Google ranks or new financial devices, and may impose bogus categories, as witch hunters and colonial racists did, with biases learned from data, as Amazon's hiring algorithm showed. The new network will be alien and fallible, so humans must stay in the loop and build institutions to catch its errors. That is a political challenge, which Part III takes up for democracy and totalitarianism.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: New technologies often bring disaster, not because they are bad but because humans take time to learn to use them. Industrial societies tried imperialism, Stalinism and Nazism before finding better ways, and humanity scraped a pass; with AI there is less room for error. Liberal democracy's strong self-correcting mechanisms are the best chance to catch mistakes, but can democracy survive the new network?

Total surveillance is possible, not inevitable: in the 1970s Denmark and Canada chose not to copy the Romanian dictatorship's informers. Four old principles can guide democracies: use data to help people, not manipulate them; never concentrate all information in one place; watch governments and corporations as closely as they watch citizens; and leave room for both change and rest, so that algorithms are neither too rigid nor too demanding. Automation threatens constant job turmoil, and common assumptions mislead: chess proved easier to automate than dish washing, and AI can read emotions. Unemployment of about 25% helped destroy the young Weimar Republic but not US democracy, which adapted through the New Deal. Yet in the 2010s and early 2020s many conservative parties, hijacked by unconservative leaders such as Donald Trump, turned revolutionary: the conservative suicide.

Self-correction needs understanding. The Topeka school board that turned away the daughter of Oliver Brown, a Black parent, was human, so its racism was plain and in 1954 the US Supreme Court struck down school segregation. COMPAS, which rated Eric Loomis, a Wisconsin defendant, high risk, kept its method a trade secret, and the makers of AlphaGo, DeepMind's go-playing AI, could not explain its move 37. Because algorithms weigh thousands of data points while humans look for a single cause, people who cannot follow them turn to conspiracy theories and charismatic leaders. A right to an explanation needs institutions that audit algorithms with computers' help, and artists who explain them, as Nosedive, an episode of the series Black Mirror, did.

Last, bots and algorithms may push the conversation into digital anarchy: bots wrote almost a fifth of tweets in one 2016 election sample, people trusted AI-made disinformation, and algorithms increasingly set the rules of debate. Democracies should outlaw counterfeit humans, as the philosopher Daniel Dennett suggests, and have a human institution vet how algorithms curate debate. Americans can no longer agree on basic facts, and nobody is sure why. If democracy collapses, it will be a failure to regulate, not technological fate.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: More than half of humanity already lives under authoritarian or totalitarian regimes, so their response to AI matters as much as that of democracies. In the 20th century totalitarianism was handicapped: the telegraph and radio could carry information to the centre, but only humans could process it, so the centre drowned in data and made errors nobody corrected. AI changes this, because more data makes algorithms better. Google, used by billions, trains better algorithms that draw still more users, and a genetic algorithm trained on China's data could pull the world's medical information there. Blockchain is no safeguard: a government with 51% of the accounts could even rewrite the past, as Caracalla, a Roman emperor, tried to erase the memory of his brother Geta.

Dictatorships have their own problems with AI. Their rule rests on terror, but a chatbot cannot be jailed or tortured. Bots may spread dissent, or develop it themselves by noticing doublespeak: Russia's constitution promises free speech, while calling the invasion of Ukraine a war is a crime. Training an algorithm to forget yesterday's official line is hard. Democracies, which tolerate more criticism, have more leeway with such rogue bots.

In the long run an algorithm might take control. Autocrats have usually been most at risk from their own subordinates. Harari imagines a Great Leader woken at four in the morning by a surveillance algorithm warning of a coup: trusting it makes him its puppet, distrusting it may get him killed. Tiberius, a Roman emperor, let all information reach him through Sejanus, commander of the Praetorian Guard, and became his puppet. Power lies where the information channels merge. In a democracy an AI would have to overcome many institutions, not one ruler.

Totalitarian regimes assume the leader is never wrong, so they are primed to trust an infallible-seeming AI and lack the mechanisms to correct it. This is the dictator's dilemma: trust AI and become its puppet, or supervise it with a human institution and limit one's own power. The weakest spot in humanity's defences may be a paranoid dictator. Yet after 1945 dictators and democracies cooperated to contain nuclear weapons, and the same is true of AI.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: Some of AI's gravest dangers arise between societies. Humanity has never been united, so a paranoid dictator who gives a fallible AI power over nuclear strikes, or terrorists who let an AI design a pandemic, could harm everyone: like climate change, AI is a global problem. Today's world of about 200 states is postimperial, and even tiny Qatar and Tuvalu have leverage. Because computers concentrate information and power, a new imperial era could begin, or humanity could split along a Silicon Curtain between rival digital empires.

Private firms led the industrial race at first, and states that ignored it, from Burma to China, were conquered or exploited. The AI race also began with companies such as Google; governments woke up when Google's AlphaGo beat Lee Sedol, the go champion, in 2016. China, scarred by what it calls the century of humiliations, vowed not to miss this train, and Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, said the AI leader would rule the world.

Empires now need data, not gunboats. Data colonies would send raw data to the hub and receive algorithms, while profits stay in San Francisco or Beijing. Land kept wealth with provincial landowners, and Britain could not move Calcutta's cotton mills; data moves at almost the speed of light, so algorithmic power can sit in one hub. Automation also threatens textile countries such as Pakistan and Bangladesh, which cannot afford to retrain workers.

China's sphere serves the state; America's serves the tech giants and protects privacy more. Because they use different software and hardware, and code and behaviour shape each other, the spheres may drift into separate cocoons, perhaps split even over the mind-body problem: are people their bodies or their online selves? Cyber weapons, stealthy and unpredictable, undermine the mutually assured destruction that kept the Cold War from turning hot.

Yet cooperation needs only the ability to exchange information. Patriotism means loving compatriots, and caring for them often requires global rules, which leave national loyalties intact, as in the World Cup. Realist thinkers such as John Mearsheimer see a law of the jungle, but real jungles are full of cooperation. War declined after 1945 because nuclear weapons raised its price, know-how could not be conquered and militarism faded, so military budgets fell to about 7% worldwide. That was a human choice, so it can be reversed, as Putin's 2022 assault on Ukraine shows; the responsibility for good choices is ours.

screens.label: The chapter in full
paragraphs: In late 2016 Harari published his book Homo Deus and, though trained in medieval and early modern military history, found himself discussing AI with scientists, entrepreneurs and leaders. Over eight years the tone changed from idle speculation to emergency. History matters because politics is about priorities, and priorities rest on readings of history, as the history lectures of Than Shwe, Myanmar's dictator, and Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, show. Leaders who expect AI to bring knowledge, as print did, or who hope to muddle through as with the Industrial Revolution, forget that those revolutions also brought witch hunts, religious wars, imperialism and Nazism.

One lesson is that new information technology always drives major change, because information weaves new networks rather than representing reality: clay tablets helped forge city-states, holy books spread religions, and newspapers and telegraphs opened the way to large-scale democracy and totalitarianism. AI may matter more than writing, because it is the first technology that makes decisions and creates ideas, and it joins every network as a member. Engineers who write its code and choose its training data are like Bishop Athanasius, a church father who helped choose the books of the Bible.

We should avoid two errors. The naive view forgets that information is not truth and that more of it can mean more witch hunts. The cynical, populist view forgets that people genuinely care about truth, as Alonso de Salazar Frías, a Spanish inquisitor, showed; because they do, conflicts can sometimes be resolved by talking and revising our stories.

Why are we so self-destructive? Not because of our nature but because our networks have privileged order over truth, gaining power without wisdom. The more powerful a network, the more it needs self-correction: humanity now resembles Tiberius, a Roman emperor, on Capri, mighty yet easily manipulated by its own creations, and a mishandled AI might put out the light of consciousness. The task is no miracle technology but the patient, ordinary work of building institutions that correct their own errors, the way life itself evolved by trial and error.
